transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Lately I just don’t care about the art shows, the mentoring, or even my photography anymore; nothing feels worth doing. My wife was the one who persuaded me to come in because I've just completely pulled back from everything.
Have you felt this way for most of the last two years, or is this a distinct change from how you were feeling a few months ago?

No, this is a very distinct change from how I used to be. These extreme swings—going from a period of intense, high energy to this heavy, joyless phase—have really only been disrupting my life for about the past five months since I retired. It is a major, sudden shift from my normal self.

During those periods of intense, high energy you mentioned, did you feel like you needed much less sleep than usual, or did you find yourself talking faster and taking on more projects than you normally would?

I was absolutely talking a mile a minute—my wife joked she couldn't get a word in edgewise during my rapid monologues. I also completely overloaded myself, cramming my calendar with endless mentoring, committee meetings, and late-night projects. I was staying up very late to work on those things, though I don't recall if I felt like I needed less sleep.
During those high-energy periods, did you feel unusually self-confident, or did others notice that your behavior was so out of character that it caused problems at work or in your relationships?

Yes, I felt incredibly self-confident, believing I was the only one who could fix those start-ups, organize the arts council, and write the definitive book on retirement strategy. This definitely strained my relationship with my wife, because I would constantly talk over her and get absolutely furious whenever she or my friends suggested I slow down or scale back. It caused a lot of tension between us because I just wouldn't listen.

During those high-energy periods, did your behavior become so extreme that you required hospitalization, or did it cause significant impairment in your ability to function at work or in your daily life?

No, I was never hospitalized, but those periods absolutely disrupted my daily life and relationships. I took on far too many overlapping projects and would get furious with my wife when she suggested I slow down, which eventually led to a complete collapse. I ended up missing a major exhibition opening I had organized and had to back out of all my mentoring commitments.

During these past five months, have you experienced any thoughts that life is not worth living, or have you felt so slowed down or physically exhausted that even simple daily tasks felt impossible to complete?

Yes, I've had dark thoughts, like wishing I wouldn't wake up or standing on the bridge by the bay wondering what it would be like to just lean forward and be done. I also feel incredibly slowed down, shuffling around and staring blankly at the kettle, so my wife has had to take over almost all of our daily household tasks because I simply can't manage.

During these recent periods where you feel slowed down and hopeless, have you noticed any physical changes like a significant loss of appetite or a complete inability to experience pleasure in activities you once loved?

I haven't really noticed any significant change in my appetite. However, I have completely lost the ability to find joy in things like my photography, mentoring, or the art shows, which now just feel like heavy chores I can't bring myself to start. It is just a profound, empty loss of interest in everything I used to love.
